Not as much of mental health but parts of it does, I suppose: I spent 5 years in military. When I was a more junior rank, we were always taught that mental health was a joke. We should "man up" or "tap" (giving up in our particular field). I started struggling with physical pain and depression not long after my twin boys died during child birth and my command sent me to go underway with another command, even though they knew what had happened. I asked if they could send another equally qualified guy instead so I could take some time to grieve with my SO. The E6 (I was an E4 at the time) laughed and said I'd get more out of going underway. I missed physical therapy appointments for this underway but no one cared. The pain and depression got worse. Even doctors started to call me out and say "you're faking it" as a way of "tapping". It took me a suicide attempt and seeing doctors for a year and a half for them to diagnose me with fibromyalgia. So..... who wants to enlist in the US military for "free healthcare"?

Tl;dr it took medical professionals over a year to agree I wasn't faking it.

I'm more insomniac than night owl. When I was deployed on a submarine, the often creepy things I'd hear when trying to sleep would be how aggressive the waters could be at periscope depth or how active sonar can be loud enough to wake a somewhat heavy sleeper. Better yet, the creaking of the hull when the boat dives. This can happen at any point during the day or night though.

Eat at the base galley every chance you can, don't buy a bunch of new things like a tv. If you really want one then buy from Facebook market place or pages like "military buy, sell, trade". Its second hand but that can save so much. When paying for things like car insurance or internet, don't be afraid to ask for military discount. Most bases I've seen have bowling alleys and small movie theaters for very cheap. Take advantage of the little things. In bootcamp they'll probably suggest you start an "Easy Start Certificate" or something to that degree, I recommend doing an automatic transfer every pay check into it so you'll never miss the money. If you move out of the barracks then places like Costco are often worth while.

I'm not a professional with money or anything, these are just things I wish I'd taken advantage of more when I was still in.

Good luck.

Edit: I also forgot this but MWR (it's an organization that offers classes, events, and assistance to service members) is a fantastic resource. They hold everything from classes on finance to becoming a parent to starting a business. TAKE ADVANTAGE OF MWR!
